subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the British North America Act, 1867, by adding thereto as part of the federal constitution, with regard to the powers of parliament, a Canadian Bill of Rights in substitution for the act of parliament, chapter 44, passed in the year 1960.
This latter statute has been to a certain point ineffective, from the fact that it is not part of the Canadian constitution and that its
application has been rather limited because most of the time the decisions of the courts have been to the effect that its provisions apply only to legislation adopted by parliament since its coming into force.
Not only new legislation but that which is already on the statute books should be interpreted in the light of the principles which will be now contained in the constitution itself, and this is what the present measure seeks to achieve.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: USE OF R.C.M.P. FILES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I stated yesterday I intended to do, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing an urgent matter of public importance, namely the misuse of secret files of the R.C.M.P. as evidenced by the public statement of Premier Lesage. He said that the R.C.M.P. security report on Mr. Vachon in the possession of the Quebec government, discloses him to be a security case. At the same time I would deal with the policy of the federal government in condoning the use of rumour and hearsay based on unproven police reports which libel the character of individuals unaccused by due process. This procedure invades despotically the legitimate rights of the individual to liberty under the law.
I do not have before me the French language version of this motion. As soon as I have it, I will make it available.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: USE OF R.C.M.P. FILES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order, please. Will the right hon. Leader of the Opposition kindly address the house on the question of urgency of debate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: USE OF R.C.M.P. FILES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will restrict myself entirely to the question of urgency. I should like to point out immediately that under our system of parliamentary government the preservation and maintenance of freedom, and any derogation from that freedom, are matters that are always urgent. Parliament will not, if it is true to its mission, allow bureaucratic practices to destroy the civil rights and the reputation of the individual. The urgency of this matter will be understood when I point out that unless this is controlled, McCarthyism and fear will be generated in the individual and, indeed, an intolerable invasion of human freedoms will result if security files can be used for political or personal vendettas.
The police state is the negation of democracy. Oligarchies of bureaucracy could, by using the security of the state as an excuse, permit the spoliation of character, the dearest possession of a human being. Discussion and public

knowledge are the only recourse and protection against uncontrolled invasions of human freedoms.
It might be argued that this question could be dealt with when the estimates come up. Your Honour I am sure will agree that if a matter like this arose in the United Kingdom the procedure at Westminster would immediately assure that the government would make available time for an early discussion. Not having that same procedure here, the only way in which it can be brought before the house without delay is to move the adjournment, which I have accordingly done on the general ground that when serious invasions affecting the rights of individuals take place the house should give first consideration thereto.

subtopic: USE OF R.C.M.P. FILES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be no doubt that the matter raised by the right hon. Leader of the Official Opposition is important and urgent. On the face of it there seems to have been a misuse of R.C.M.P. files, such a file having been used by the premier of Quebec to discredit Mr. Arthur Yachon, who was president of the Quebec provincial police association. It certainly would be a serious thing if in this country premiers or any other persons in government were allowed to use R.C.M.P. files in order to discredit organizations with which they had a difference of opinion. Therefore this is a matter of great import not only to this house but to the people of Canada.
It seems to me that the urgency of debate would lie in the fact that this motion will give the Prime Minister and the ministers more directly responsible an opportunity first to give the facts to the house and consequently to indicate when these files were made available to provincial authorities; and second, to inform us as to why they were given and what protection is provided by way of an insistence that these files shall be used only for prosecutions and surveillance under due process of law.
If Your Honour decides that this matter is sufficiently urgent to allow the government to make a statement, then we will welcome it. If Your Honour decides it is not of sufficient urgency to call for a debate of this kind, I certainly hope the government will either call the estimates of the Solicitor General or that the Prime Minister will provide some opportunity so he can assure the house and the country that there will be no repetition of what appears to have been a disgraceful misuse of public, confidential documents.
June 2. 1966

It seems to me that, if there were any urgency, Mr. Vachon could have engaged immediate proceedings against the premier of Quebec. Now, he stated himself that he was postponing this until after the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO AGENDA

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I did have it ready yesterday, but I do not think my hon. friend was in the house when I was in a position to give a reply. Therefore perhaps he will forgive me if I am a day late in respect of that reply, which is to confirm what is already known to the house, that the federal-provincial conference will take place on June 16 and 17 as part of the commemoration of the centenary of the union of British Columbia and the island of Vancouver.
The main item on the agenda will be the question of federal assistance to university financing. None of the provinces has proposed that any other item be added to the agenda although they, as well as the federal government, will still be free to raise in the usual way questions of particular concern to them under the item "Other Matters".
As the conference will be only a day and a half in length, and part of that time will be devoted to ceremonials, it is not likely that we would have much time to deal with other matters because one item on the agenda is of such great importance.
Perhaps the house would be interested to know that my colleagues the two ministers from British Columbia will represent the federal government with me at the various ceremonies. In view of the nature of the agenda other federal ministers attending will be the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State, the President of the Privy Council and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to voice my protest against the designated area policy of the government. In fact it is a policy which should not be entertained by the Department of Industry at all.
When making an assessment of any policy one usually divides it into two parts, one showing the advantages and the other the disadvantages. This I have done. In the advantages column the only merit of a policy of this type that I can see is that it provides a certain amount of relief to unemployment, which has nothing to do with the Department of Industry.
The disadvantages are many. The results of this policy so far as industry is concerned include discrimination between communities, patronage on a large scale, subsidizing inefficient operations, increasing the cost of production with increases in taxes for those who pay taxes, creation of municipal problems that did not exist previously, creation of new industrial problems that industry did not have to contend with previously, curtailment of the nation's natural economic development, an adverse effect on the problems of our competitive position with regard to world markets, a further contribution to the problem of inflation which the government is trying to combat and, lastly, such a program and policy hinder normal industrial development.
When the minister presented his estimates he stated some sound principles which we hoped his department would follow. I suggest to him that if his department had followed those principles in regard to the policy of designated areas I would not be standing on my feet today. The implication of such a
Supply-Industry
designated area policy is actually contrary to the principles enunciated by the minister. The whole program of designated areas has the opposite effect to what the minister is trying to achieve, if we are to go by the principles he has outlined.
As recorded at page 5374 of Hansard for May 20 the minister said:
The department was established in recognition of the pressing need for Canada to attain an efficient expansion of our manufacturing industries.
How can industry attain efficient expansion when the government bribes industries to locate in areas where it is less efficient for them to operate?
The reason I use the word "bribe" is that another hon. member, when speaking on the minister's estimates, said that in his constituency an industry had been closed because it refused to move to a new site in Montreal. This was said the last time the minister's estimates were before the house. It was stated that the industry in question would not be given contracts unless it moved to Montreal. If this is not bribery I do not know what is.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Another statement made by the minister was that "we must at the same time ensure that industrial efficiency improves". I suggest that the present designated area program does not lend itself to improved efficiency in any way. In fact, it is a retrograde policy delaying the improvements which industry realizes it must achieve for competitive reasons. A perfect example of such retrogression took place in my own community as a result of this ill-conceived policy. I believe the minister is aware of it. It has to do with an asbestos plant that was going to locate in my own constituency, indeed, in my own home town. The industry had decided to locate in this place because of three main factors, ample water supplies, ideal waste disposal facilities, and close proximity to the American market which it hoped to develop. However, because of a saving of half a million dollars, in fact, closer to three-quarters of a million dollars, I believe, in capital expenditure and because of the fast write-off, the industry located elsewhere as a result of the government incentive to do so.
It can easily be seen that the result in that case is contrary to the principle the minister laid down and will not bring about the improvement in efficiency he wishes to achieve. Certainly this industry cannot be as efficient in the new location as it would have been had it been able to locate where the

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
three factors necessary to the industry were available. The industry, in order to take advantage of the incentive under this program, the $600,000 and the fast write-off, took a short-term view of its future and decided to locate elsewhere. I suggest to the minister that because of the designated area policy industry today throughout the whole of Canada is taking a short-range view with respect to location, which in the future could be detrimental to Canada.
In his opening remarks the minister also stated that the aim of the Department of Industry is to ensure that this influence is positive and helpful. I ask the minister to tell me, on the basis of his experience already with the designated area policy, helpful to whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: To Canada.

In respect of the case I have just cited the minister has not been very helpful so far as our community and that industry are concerned. He certainly has not been helpful to the municipality affected because at the place where this industry was going to locate provision had been made to absorb the additional children there would be in that area. In the area where the company is now going there will be a great many problems. Problems are being created where they did not exist before. This may apply only to small communities, but if the minister wants diversification of industry this is where industry must go rather than be centralized in the large centres.
I suggest to the minister that it is not a positive program as has been stated by him, but a negative one. If the minister allows the designated area program to continue he will be creating new problems which some future government will have to solve. Possibly the minister has the idea that the present government is not going to be in office too long and is creating these problems for a future government. In other words, and I am not being facetious, I think the minister will realize that the problems I am outlining certainly will become major ones in the not too distant future. I say that if the minister was honest in his presentation of these estimates he would say that his designated area program was not designed to benefit industry in the first place. As I said before, the program is an effort on the part of the government to deal with the unemployment problem which should have been left with the Department of Labour.

I would ask the minister and the government to study closely the words of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. The article in the Saint John Times-Globe of May 19, from which he quoted, referred to the Atlantic provinces but it could apply to the prairie provinces as well. It points out the harmful effect on communities, not only harmful at present but for the future also, of such a program. The article is worth repeating and I take the liberty of doing so now. The article reads as follows:
Denial of the incentives is crippling the centres that could lead these provinces in an economic renaissance . . . Established industries have moved out of these centres to get aid; potential new ones have been lost. The cities are being bled in the name of healing and the whole region is weakened.
Former speakers have also stated, and I think the minister must have taken note of this, that the formula he is using is absolutely wrong. The last time the minister's estimates were before the house I believe the hon. member for Provencher said that the formula as the minister had enunciated it was not even being followed. As I understood the information given to the house, it was based on unemployment figures as well as family income figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Non-farm family income.

So far as I am concerned the formula is wrong because, as other members have pointed out, the unemployment and home income figures used do not apply in the same way in each province. In one example in respect of Manitoba I believe it was pointed out that in the case of one designated area where an industry was allowed to locate and get the incentives, the income figure was larger than in other areas in the same province. In my view the formula had not been followed in that instance.
Before these estimates are passed I hope the minister will give a commitment to the house that he will do away with this program at this time. If he would do so, I do not think he would have any difficulty in getting his estimates through.

Mr. Chairman, the minister's estimates are now before the committee and I intend to keep my remarks relatively brief and related to a subject on which I have been dealing with the minister for a number of months now. It is a happy coincidence that I can bring it up at this time because the minister has under his jurisdiction the National Research Council, the Department of
June 2, 1968

Defence Production and the Department of Industry. These three agencies of government relate to the subject I wish to touch upon briefly this afternoon, a subject with which the minister has dealt ably in so many ways over the past months.
Research, the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Industry are all related to the problem of automobile safety and highway safety. Over the past months much has been done in these three departments in this regard. I repeat that I intend to keep my remarks on this subject relatively short this afternoon. I think all members of the House of Commons, together with the people of Canada, have come to recognize that the problem of automobile and highway safety and automobile and highway deaths and injuries constitutes a national and international epidemic. The automobile is the greatest killer of young people between the ages of 18 and 35 and the third greatest killer of all our people, exceeded only by heart disease and cancer. We recognize that we have an epidemic involving the driver as the agent, the road as the atmosphere and the car as the microbe, and that we must approach the problem in a scientific, epidemiological way.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There is a problem of jurisdiction involved, and the minister has mentioned this before various house committees. Provincial governments must educate better and safer drivers. They must continue to build better and safer roads and they must insist on regular and meaningful annual or semi-annual inspections of automobiles. While the federal government can help with uniform codes and take the lead in this regard with the approbation of the provinces, all these matters do fall under provincial jurisdiction constitutionally.
We are able to refer to this subject today during the consideration of the minister's estimates because I firmly believe that the federal government alone can bring the construction of automobiles under the rule of law. Whether we are talking about the matter in a legal or constitutional sense, certainly in a realistic sense the United States found that only the federal government can invoke uniform standards relating to the production of safer automobiles at the manufacturing level or on import. It is in relation to the minister's responsibility for industry that I refer to this subject under these estimates today.
Supply-Industry
I am fully aware of the fact that the classic role of the Minister of Industry is to assist and encourage industry to expand, develop and do a generally good job in Canada. In looking at things in detail one realizes that the Minister of Industry is placed in a difficult position, and I imagine the government has recognized the jurisdictional problem facing it in formulating mandates with regard to scientifically proven safety standards in the automobile industry at the production stage.
We have now reached the question whether it is the Minister of Industry, the Minister of Transport or the Minister of National Health and Welfare who should enforce standards. I say on an optimistic note that some agency of government is going to have to invoke mandatory standards of safety in the automobile industry within a very few months.
We have talked about what provincial governments can do. I firmly believe that if the federal governments of the United States and Canada live up to their responsibilities, with the co-operation of opposition members, the public and the industry, and state to the industry that it must put already scientifically proven safety features in automobiles at the production stage, this one step alone will cut highway deaths and injuries by 50 per cent. That does not mean to say that we should neglect the problems associated with developing better drivers, better roads and annual inspections of automobiles at the provincial level, but I wash to emphasize the real role the federal government must play in this regard.
I should like to congratulate the minister for the initiative he has already shown and for his efforts which have led to the convening of a conference of provincial authorities in the near future on the subject of automobile safety. I certainly hope that at that time the problem of jurisdiction can be ironed out. In my opinion it will be relatively simple to iron out the problem because the federal government already has jurisdiction over foods and drugs and in respect of issuing mandates as to safety standards for aircraft, ships and rolling stock on the railways. No matter what the constitutional or legal position is, I think it is going to be a relatively easy job for the federal government to get approbation from the provinces to act as a central authority with respect to mandates as to safety standards right across the nation in terms of telling the industry that it must put scientifically proven safety features in automobiles at the manufacturing level.

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
I want to note two recommendations contained in the brief in this regard which was presented to the Prime Minister after the terrible slaughter that took place on our highways last year on the July 1st week end. Before doing so I want to thank the members of all parties who have endorsed this brief and the people who spent so much time in researching it and helping me to put it together.
One of the recommendations was that the government act immediately to create and establish a national accident research centre. One reason we have made so few inroads in terms of combating this international epidemic is that we know very little about it. Once an accident has taken place we do not know too much about what has caused a death or injury.
What happened in respect of the air accident at Ste Therese a little over two years ago which killed over 100 people? We immediately roped off the site of the accident and, at a cost to the federal treasury of between $4 million and $5 million, we put the aircraft together bit by bit and held a judicial inquiry with the result that we got some information which will help us to reduce the number of similar accidents in the future.
Every holiday week end in Canada over 100 people are killed on our highways. Within 10 or 15 minutes of the accident the morgue wagon takes the corpses to a morgue or funeral parlour, as the case may be, and the automobiles are towed to the junk heap. We know nothing about what happened in terms of the reason for an accident which has caused death or injury. Not one cent of private or public money is spent on research to find out what happened. When we are travelling in aircraft-the minister and I have chatted about this-we are 10 times as safe as when we are travelling on the highways.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I think it is six times.

I suggest it is approximately 10 times as safe. Why is that the case? In Canada and in the United States millions and millions of dollars are spent on licensing safe pilots, building safe aircraft at the production stage and providing federal inspectors who tell the aircraft companies what safety features must be included in aircraft at the production stage, just as we do in respect of ships and rolling stock.
We spend millions of dollars in formulating and enforcing safe aircraft rules; yet the simple automobile, in which all of us here

today will ride at some time or another, falls outside the rule of law. I do not believe that the people of Canada or the United States people are going to tolerate jurisdictional disputes between the provinces or states and the federal government while the automobile remains outside the rule of law.
We have discovered that very little private money is being spent on research in this regard. In 1964 in the United States Senator Kennedy obtained information in the U.S. senate commerce committee to the effect that General Motors of the United States had made a profit of $1,700 million but had only spent approximately $1,250,000 on safety research.
What happened in 1952 or 1956-I am not sure of the year-in regard to polio? We spent millions of dollars on research in respect of the epidemic and had the co-operation of all governments, scientific people, legislators and the public. Yet even at its worst the polio epidemic only killed between 2 per cent and 4 per cent of the number of lives that are claimed annually on our highways. We spent millions of dollars in research in respect of that epidemic and we licked it. Yet we spend nothing to conquer the greatest killer of our young people and the third greatest killer of our population at large. We are going to have to increase our research spending in this regard and we must have a national research centre.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Would it be too much, for instance, to ask that before July 1 next we say to every police officer in Canada: Make a meaningful report on death-producing accidents. Tell us something about the driver. Tell us something about the immediate circumstances in which he found himself before he became involved in the death-producing accident. What kind of vehicle was he driving? Why did he get into the accident? What kind of road was he on? What caused death or injury to him?
We know nothing about these matters now. Would it be too much to ask that the wrecks of cars involved in accidents be brought to a national research centre and that photographs of these wrecks be taken. Various farsighted coroners throughout the North American continent descend immediately on death-producing accidents and get the real facts and meaningful data which show why the accident occurred and why injury or death was caused.
June 2. 1966

I believe that a national accident research centre, not only for research into automobile accidents but other matters connected with accidents, would go a long way to help us move forward in this regard. It is largely because of the little bit of research being done at the U.C.L.A., Harvard and Cornell crash research centres that I and many others interested in this field sincerely feel that if safety standards for automobiles were controlled by mandate at the production level, this would cut the death and injury rate by approximately 50 per cent provided the provincial authorities co-operate at the same time in the other areas of safety in terms of the driver, roads and annual inspection of vehicles.
The second suggestion I make is this. Today the minister has under his jurisdiction many officials who are drafting safety codes in the area of automobiles, roads, and drives. My remarks as a federal legislator will relate only to the automobile. These codes are now being drafted, as the minister has informed the house on many occasions, under the aegis of the Department of Defence Production. It is my impression that the sooner some public authority builds a prototype safety car the better.
I am not going into the question of blame. I feel that the industry in years ahead will sell just as many safe cars as it is selling stylish cars today. I believe that safety can be sold Whether it can be sold or not, I believe it is incumbent upon the industry in our modern society to include safety features in its products. I believe a prototype safety car must be built by public authority. Members might ask me why. I remember that when we testified in New York a few months ago, the same night the industry made the announcement relating to collapsible steering columns and double-braking systems in cars. No doubt this will be an advance in this regard. I am not competent enough, nor do I know enough about the details, to make an objective judgment on whether this will be really significant. But I will say, and not in a dramatic, accusing way, that I believe the advances we will see in the 1967 models have been known to the industry for approximately ten years.
Suppose the food industry tomorrow morning at nine o'clock said to the government: We will be good little boys and take a little bit of poison out of the food the public have been eating for years and years. Legislators and the public at large would then have the
Supply-Industry
right to ask how much poison was in the food in the past and how much was to be left in it in the future. Until governments and public authorities set up criteria based on prototype standards which they develop and correlate, we cannot make a correct judgment in this regard.
People sometimes think it is dramatic to take the position of whipping the big boys in industry, but I am not trying to do that. But at the same time I do not think anything as important and big as the automobile industry can be left to police itself any more than we can leave the food and drug industries to police themselves. So I believe that, first, standards must be mandatory and must be based on code regulations. If these code regulations are to be really meaningful, they must be based on objective criteria put together by governments.
This is why I believe that a prototype safety car must be built by a public authority. I would encourage the minister to do everything humanly possible to take the lead in this regard and offer Canadian aid, whether by direct financial assistance or co-operation by the National Research Council in respect of research projects, to bring the New York prototype safety car project to a successful conclusion as soon as possible.
I have referred to the New York prototype safety car. Many people ask me, "Why can't we do it in Canada" or, "Why can't it be done somewhere else?" Mr. Chairman, highway and automobile safety know no party or national boundaries. It is an international epidemic that we face. In my view the government of the state of New York is the only one in the western world that has made any real advances in terms of bringing such a car to completion. It has spent a couple of hundred thousand dollars in getting feasibility studies through the lower and upper houses in New York state and having them approved. It is interesting that an aircraft space agency has the contract to build the first seven prototype safety cars and crash them. I appeal to all hon. members; Let us move in this regard.
We are living in 1966, a year in which we can put men into orbit around the earth and bring them back, when we can almost put them on the moon and bring them back in safety. Yet we permit this slaughter to continue on our highways. Can we not stop it? I think we can if the government acts, and it can act even before Washington. Everybody says: Does it matter what Canada does? The

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
United States will do something in this respect and whatever they do will affect us. I think we hold-the minister can correct me here if I am wrong-between 7 per cent and 10 per cent of the North American automobile market. If the government and the minister took the lead in this regard the industry would pay a great deal of attention.
In the United States, the G.S.A. fixed standards in this respect. The federal government there purchases approximately 50,000 to 55,000 vehicles a year. By fixing standards for government-purchased vehicles the United States woke up the industry. Surely if Canada co-operated with New York, which has a population almost as large as that of our country and involving about 20 per cent of the automobile market, we would certainly make the industry look up and take notice.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I believe it is imperative, first that we move quickly to establish a national research centre of this type and, second, that we co-operate as quickly as possible with New York in the completion of a prototype safety car. Canada can take a real lead in this regard. Would it be too much to ask that this be done? Have we not the technical know-how to conduct meaningful research at the present time if we from next January 1 collect all automobiles that are involved in death-producing accidents and tell police officers to give us the type of meaningful report to which I have referred?
Police officers have a very difficult task in this regard. When a car is involved in a death-producing accident the police officer usually has several important things to do. He has to get the body to the morgue and the automobile off the road so that traffic may start flowing again. Under present-day circumstances it is almost too much to ask him to fill out a meaningful report which would help us correlate and centralize data that we could use in research. I want to congratulate some of the more forward-looking coroners and police officers in Canada who are making initial and pioneering attempts in this regard. Some day we will have ratings for automobiles, whether the industry likes it or not. When we buy an automobile we will know which are safe and which are not as safe. Police officers will look at cars that have caused a death and note the mileage. They will record how many miles the car had been driven and how many such vehicles were sold and registered at a particular time. We will have safety ratings on cars.

People have come to me and said, "Grafftey, you are crazy. If I want to drive an unsafe car, that is my business in a free world." It is nobody's business in a free world to drive an unsafe car. You can kill yourself if you want to but you cannot go out on the highways and kill innocent women and children who may be involved in an accident with you. When we consider that 87 per cent of all injury and death-producing accidents occur at speeds under 45 miles per hour, it is my belief that the federal governments of Canada and the United States have a real role to play in bringing the automobile under the rule of law immediately.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The minister has already done much in that respect. I repeat that it is my belief that the next two things to which priority should be given are the establishment of a national research centre and the completion of the building of a prototype safety car. I am sure that as we move ahead in this regard the minister will have the co-operation of every member of the house.

Mr. Chairman, I have been quite impressed by what has been said by the member for Brome-Missisquoi on the subject of automobile safety. It is something to which most people do not give much consideration until it is too late. It is too late to do anything after a calamity has befallen you or a member of your family has had a bad accident.
In his book Ralph Nader states facts implicating the automobile industry in abuses. I was particularly impressed by the example he gave of a woman driving down a street in a Corvair at a speed of less than 30 miles an hour and the car went out of control and rolled over. She lost her arm as a result. All this happened when she was driving at a speed at which one would have said it would be impossible to upset a car no matter what one did. Everyone who reads this story will probably think immediately of the criminal negligence that must take place in the automobile industry.
Of course most people do not think about safety. I presume if we really considered it seriously we would not drive. We are all aware of the fact that when you drive down a very busy highway and see an ambulance and a number of vehicles around a bad accident, traffic slows down to a crawl for 10 to 20 miles. But memory is very short and soon thereafter the previous speed is resumed.
June 2, 1966

At one time I was driving a new Meteor in northern Ontario on roads that were mainly unpaved. Most of the time I drove at high speed. Every 200 or 300 miles I had to stop at a garage and have the shock absorbers in the rear end of the car repaired. One day the mechanics fixed the shock absorbers-they welded in new plates and tore pieces out of the frame, etc.

and after they put the car back together I noticed that the shock absorbers did not extend sufficiently to allow for a connection. Actually they did not have enough distance between them to allow for full play and every time the springs extended to their full capacity the shock absorbers proved to be about four inches too short. In discussion with the representative of the Ford Motor Company I found out that this was certainly a problem but it was not the responsibility of the company to do something about it. What had happened was that the model had been changed and the shock absorbers did not fit the new model. They were obviously not built for that car. It was a leased car and I refused to drive it any further because of its unsatisfactory condition. Later on a man was killed in it. I am sure that its poor condition was not only due to the fact that, as the police found out, the speedometer was registering 15 miles an hour below the actual speed so that when I thought I was driving at 70 miles an hour I was actually going about 90.
No wonder I was having trouble with the car. In my opinion the shock absorbers were not built for the car. I presume this was the case in most of the cars in that series. The engineer of the Ford Motor Company in charge of maintenance was not the least bit interested in doing anything about that particular car and was prepared to admit that the shock absorbers were not appropriate. However, he was not willing to make recommendations for improvements.
It seems to me that Ralph Nader probably dealt with only a very limited number of real problems. I think the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi will be remembered in Canada for quite some time if he is able to bring the attention of a sufficient number of thinking Canadians to this problem. The automobile industry has been able to get away with a lot of ballyhoo on expensive radio and television programs instead of producing a piece of satisfactorily engineered equipment.
Supply-Industry
I think the matter of safety is one that affects Canada and that there should be legislation. The hon. member mentioned the fact that the state of New York is far ahead of all other areas in the matter of safety and is spending money on the building of a prototype car. I think that Canada, even with its limited resources, should be able to spend $1 million to have the National Research Council do work on this project.
The National Research Council need not work along the same lines as the state of New York but could do research of its own. I do not suggest that we should build tanks to ensure safety on the road because we would then have to instal so much equipment in the form of safety belts and so on that the purpose would be defeated because nobody would use them. I know this is a problem. I have a shoulder harness in my Volvo automobile but I never use it. My son tells me it is very good. At one time he was in a car which overturned and probaby that is why he now says the harness works very well and is very comfortable. I think this is a psychological problem. I do not think it will be solved by putting people in safety helmets and giving them football uniforms to withstand the shock of an accident. It would be better to eradicate unsafe projections in cars.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It seems to me the National Research Council might also take a look at a number of other causes of accidents in Canada. There is a stretch of highway No. 17 west of North Bay leading to Sudbury on which probably more deaths have occurred than in any other area. Some of the trouble seems to stem from the fact that the very white concrete absorbs the light, and the road is also very straight. The road is built in concrete sections 20 to 40 feet in length and a continuous noise is created as tires pass over the joints. The white line dividing the highway creates another problem. The types of lights used and the desirability of having automatic dimming devices and more readily accessible types of controls are factors which should be taken into account. Certainly correction of these faults must be taken into account by any person driving an automobile, and protection in this regard must be provided to those driving cars in our nation.
I was very surprised at the ignorant attitude publicly displayed by the president of the Chrysler Corporation who, in referring to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, said, "Who ever heard of him? What does he know

June 2. 1966
Supply-Industry
about automobiles?" Many people do not know the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. People tend to be more familiar with members from their own part of the country and less familiar with members from other parts of the country. They do not have a national outlook. However, when the president of the Chrysler Corporation singled out the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi he did two things. First of all, he made people aware of the fight taking place not only in Canada but elsewhere with regard to automobile safety. He made people aware, for example, of Senator Kennedy's interest and those interested in university safety programs, including Ralph Nader and others. Like many other people, having heard of the problems that exist I read Ralph Nader's book on automobile safety. Having read it I am convinced that much can be done.
Another thing that the president of the Chrysler Corporation did was to make people examine the silly argument used by the automobile industry that the fault lies not with the automobile but with the driver. I agree that if the automobile were left in the driveway nothing would happen. None the less, not all accidents happen at 100 miles an hour; not all accidents happen in adverse weather conditions. If accidents occurred under such conditions, with the driver also intoxicated or overly fatigued because of long driving, there might be some argument for the automobile industry. Nevertheless, when a person sitting beside the driver hits his head on the radio control panel or on another instrument and is killed, that does not indicate that that person was drunk, fatigued or anything else. It indicates that the automobile was poorly designed.
If the automobile industry gave away its automobiles there might be some excuse for some of the things said. But it charges a fantastic amount of money for automobiles. The Canadian government gets in taxes about one-third of the money from automobile sales. It therefore has a major responsibility to see that the Canadian public is not being hosed. The government does not take its responsibilities seriously. We are willing to give the automobile companies $50 million. For what, may I ask, Mr. Chairman? Certainly not for safety.
When we talk about safety in terms of $100,000 the government is still not willing to provide it. I hope that the committee will take a look at this problem even though the

minister has not looked into it. In this connection I heard an extraordinarily silly argument in committee this morning. An official of the department said that the house would not grant more money for such purposes. These estimates have not been reduced. If we had reduced them we would probably have an election because a want of confidence motion would be involved.
How would you vote on the want of confidence motion?

I know how I should vote. In the past we have reduced items in the estimates to $1, and the hon. gentleman asking the question was on the other side of the house at that time. I am sure he voted the opposite way to me. It all depends on what you are reducing and who is doing the reducing.
If the minister asked for another $100,000 for purposes of safety, I am sure that no member of parliament would oppose his request. Perhaps the minister will stand up and tell us why he has not asked for this money. Is a jurisdictional problem involved? Does it not come under his department? Frankly, I am not sure whether it should not come under the National Research Council. I know that the Minister of Industry has some interest in the automobile industry but I am not sure of the exact jurisdictional boundary. In any event, will the minister give specific answers to the questions that have been asked? I am prepared to agree to the voting of an increase of $100,000 in these estimates if the minister will ask for that sum.
I should also be prepared to support the hon. member who just asked a question if he desired to request that $100,000 be added to the estimates for an automobile safety program. Frankly, I do not know how it could be done because if the hon. member were to do so he might be out of order, but if the minister did so it might be in order. Fundamentally it depends on whether the minister feels that such a program is worth undertaking and, second, whether he has the jurisdiction to do what I suggest. I think we should know the answer to that.
There are other problems I should like to raise but other members may wish to comment on the very important matter raised by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. I should therefore like to give other hon. members and the minister in particular an opportunity to delve into this problem. I hope the minister will inform us fully how we can go
June 2, 1966

about establishing an automobile safety program, whether he is prepared to support such a program and, if necessary, whether he is prepared to move an amendment to these estimates to make such a program possible.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to take a few moments of the time of the committee. First of all, I endorse 100 per cent what the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi has said concerning the need for an automobile safety program in this country. I commend his words very strongly to the minister. I hope the government will have the good sense to take his thoughtful suggestions seriously and to act on them. I too have given this matter serious thought, as I am sure all other hon. members have.
I want to speak for a few moments about another subject. I refer to automation. Whether we like it or not, automation is going to play an increasingly important role in our lives from now on.
As we know, Mr. Chairman, automation produces greater efficiency and greater productivity, thereby lowering costs and lowering selling prices. Automation should make it possible to increase sales greatly, both here in Canada and in the export market, through lower selling prices. But if these increased sales are not sufficient to provide enough additional jobs to absorb those who lose their employment through automation, mass unemployment could develop as a result. It would then be a dismal failure.
Automation will be a success from the national point of view if we can teach the people who are displaced the skills they will need to fit them for the more technical jobs which automation will make available to them. The benefits of change will be fully and properly shared only if we consider the needs of the people who are affected by automation and if we organize our policies in such a way as to reduce hardship and insecurity to an absolute minimum.
I think we all agree that no humane society can permit workers to be made jobless on a large scale through no fault of their own. Our future success as an industrial nation is going to depend on the way we are able to plan both on the national and on the company level to provide our people with the opportunities of acquiring the skills necessary to enable them to take their place in the technical world in which they are going to live.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I believe that the government has a very real responsibility in this regard and that it
Supply-Industry
must set an example to Canadian industry by the way it treats its employees who are affected by automation in their direct employment by the government, or as employees of the crown corporations which are creatures of the government. In order to do so, I believe that the government would do well to study what is being done in this regard by large United States companies which are giving great leadership in this matter.
I was very much impressed, Mr. Chairman, by the description of the responsibility of industry in this regard which was given by Mr. Clarence B. Randall, the recently retired chairman of the Inland Steel Corporation of the United States. He described this responsibility of industry in the following words:
Our responsibility is to prepare the man who is being displaced for another task that will require a higher level of skill and which will exist after the change in the method of production takes place.
In the United States, Mr. Chairman, individual companies and unions have made considerable progress in this connection. For instance, the Kaiser Steel Corporation and the United Steelworkers have agreed that displaced workers should be guaranteed salaries up to three years and placed on an employment reserve. Another example is given by the Armour Meat Packing Company and its several unions. They have set up a fund between them to study the effects of automation on the employees of the company and to retrain affected workers.
These, Mr. Chairman, are merely two examples of the kind of forward-looking steps which Canadian companies should be taking at this time so that the steady transfer to the more automated society in which we are going to be living in the future may proceed without causing hardship to those displaced through no fault of their own. Therefore I strongly urge the government to give leadership to all Canadian companies in the interests of their workers, the companies themselves, and the country. I urge the government and these Canadian companies to follow the excellent example set by companies such as those in the United States which I have mentioned, thereby making the transition to an automated society in Canada as easy as possible.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I believe that such an attitude and such a program are the least we can do for our fellow workers as we move together along the road to progress.
