speechtext:
Shall the item carry?

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry

No, Mr. Chairman. I would hope that the minister would answer some of the questions which have been asked before this vote carries. When he does answer, would he differentiate between what he terms a rural family income and an urban family income? Does he realize that what might well be called an urban family income in Quebec and Ontario cannot be looked at in the same way in the west? The radius of service of a community is much greater in the west than in this part of the country. For example, cities in eastern Canada may be five to six times larger than communities in the west and service a very small area whereas in the west a town of 15,000 can serve a radius of 100 miles. Perhaps the minister will explain the formula he uses, which I say is discriminatory.
I hope the minister will also give a commitment in regard to discontinuing the designated area program. It is doing nothing but hurting the economy of the country and it will do greater damage in the future.
I observe that the hon. member for Peterborough is now present and I should like to say that I was quite taken by his speech except for one part to which I should now like to refer. He said that he had had excellent co-operation and so had the people from his area who had come to Ottawa to inquire how industry could co-operate with the Department of Industry.
I am sure it is not the minister's intention that industry from the various regions should come to Ottawa to co-operate with the Department of Industry. My idea is exactly the converse, that the Department of Industry was set up to help industry. In view of the hon. member's remarks I would ask, if it is the opinion of the government that industry should come to Ottawa and try to help the department? If so, what is the use of the department? Is it just a fulfilment of Parkinson's law where you have civil servants doing something just for the sake of doing it, and that is all?
I would also ask the minister to explain to the committee how the designated area policy is helping industry. What are the results of the policy? As I said before, it is of assistance to the unemployment situation but it does not solve the unemployment problem at all. Perhaps it just moves the problem from one area to another.
Because of the instigation of the designated area policy by the minister, people in certain regions of the country now find that their
[The Deputy Chairman.]
incomes are decreasing as a result of the intervention of the minister's policy. I do not think this is fair to the people in these regions. I would ask the minister to make the commitment now that he will discontinue the designated area policy. I see that the minister is shaking his head, indicating a negative reply. Therefore I would ask him to give the committee his reason before this item passes.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. At the beginning I should like to thank the minister for receiving all the delegations I have brought to Ottawa to see him when we were pressing for the inclusion of northwestern Ontario and the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River in the ADA program.
Were you successful?

Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, we were unsuccessful in getting our area designated. In one particular case an industry claimed it would only come there if the ADA program were extended to the area, but when it was not it came there any way, which proves to a certain extent that in my area we may be suffering from some sort of inferiority complex.
I have one suggestion I would put before the minister, and I realize that there are constitutional obstructions in the way. I believe that when the ADA program was first brought down it was instituted for the specific purpose of helping to cure the problem of unemployment, which at the time was quite rife throughout the country. I think this has been accomplished to a large extent. Our economists and statistical staff tell us that in certain industries we are suffering from a form of overemployment. In other words, there are now labour shortages.
However, there are areas, such as our natural resource areas, where this does not hold true at all. There are people there who are unskilled and do not have the necessary mobility to move around. If they do have this mobility the effect is that they move to other areas, with a consequent lack of population in areas such as mine which has a low unemployment record because those who are unemployed leave the area. This is very unhealthy. It hurts our economic growth and makes it more difficult for new industries or for a new mine to open in the area in order to bring people back to fill the jobs which would be created and which are already available.
June 2. 1966

I have two suggestions to make. First of all,
I should like to see the ADA program, now that its primary purpose has been accomplished, expanded and become some sort of program to encourage economic growth in areas such as Kenora-Rainy River, northwestern Ontario and other regions not directly adjacent to economic areas such as Winnipeg, Montreal and Toronto.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
My second point, though perhaps this is not the appropriate place to make it, is that in my area there is a very large Indian population. These people are untrained for work. Nevertheless there are examples in my riding as well as in other parts of the country where, with the proper supervision and training, such people can be absorbed into industry. Perhaps the Department of Industry could look into the possibility of providing training programs, or introductory programs, to help our Indian people. While there is a shortage of skilled workmen in our area there is a tremendous surplus of unskilled workmen, most of them Indians. It will be impossible to integrate these native people into our society unless we are able to provide for them the necessary economic incentives.
I fully realize that activities of this kind must be carried out in co-operation with the provinces concerned and that sometimes the provinces are not very co-operative. If the provincial minister responsible for this important type of development is not ready to work with the federal authority, then the effect in a province such as my own can only be deplorable. Nevertheless I would urge the minister to investigate the possibility of extending the program so as to fill the gap which now exists.
I turn now to consider a further problem which has arisen in my area. As a result of the regional development policies of the Ontario government we are included in an organization called the Northwest Ontario Development Corporation. The fact which faces us is that Winnipeg in another province is our natural economic centre. Thus there is a conflict between ordinary economic forces and political forces, and this makes things extremely difficult.
I know that the minister is fully aware of the situation. He has written voluminous letters to myself, to Senator Benidickson and to others who are interested. I leave these thoughts with him in the hope that in the future an alternative arrangement may be worked out.
Supply-Industry

Mr. Chairman, industry is for various reasons, a matter of interest in the region where I come from. The first one is that we are expecting an industrial explosion in the next few years, thanks to the announcement made by the provincial government about the establishment of the steel plant to be called Sidbec. Also, because we are one of the most important distribution centres of electrical power in Canada. In addition, we have six technical schools training skilled workers, which will make things easier for the industries coming to settle in our region. We have industrial commissions and we followed with great interest the legislation passed here in 1963.
I must say at this time that we are happy about the minister's intervention in the field of industry. We had the opportunity to congratulate the government in this regard. I am not trying to flatter it and I will make three or four constructive criticisms in that spirit later on.
I think that the legislation dealing with the designated areas should be amended right now; it probably did some good when it was implemented, but the time has come to revise it in the light of new conditions. Some things which seem illogical are happening. Here is a case in particular. In my region, more exactly in the city of Cap-de-la-Madeleine, a neighbour of Trois-Rivieres, the following incident happened a few weeks ago.
The members of the industrial board of the city of Shawinigan, located in the riding next to that of Champlain, lured an industry away from Cap-de-la-Madeleine, which is not yet in my riding but will be at the next election, it seems to me that this industry moved precisely because of the fiscal advantages offered in the so-called designated areas. I find it strange that this legislation can succeed in getting an industry to move such a short distance away, that is 15 miles from us, solely it seems because of the fiscal advantages it found in Shawinigan, at the heart of a designated area. Was the region made a designated area because the hon. member for Shawinigan is the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance or because before that he was the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister? I am not blaming the people of Shawinigan for looking after their own interests; I am not blaming the hon. member for using his influence. I am talking

June 2, 1866
Supply-Industry
about the legislation as objectively as possible. I mentioned the case to illustrate what I mean.
I studied closely the standards which determine the choice of a designated area. It seems to me that something is wrong with regard to the region I represent, that is Trois-Rivieres, Cap-de-la-Madeleine. We are supposed to be one of the cities where the average salary is the highest in Canada. We come in fourth or fifth place, but that does not give the whole picture. If we got that far, that is the fourth or fifth place as far as the average salary is concerned, it is due to the paper industry which pays higher than average salaries. The fact is that a large number of our wage-earners draw less than average wages and that we have a greater percentage of out-of-work people than in neighbouring constituencies.
The conditions are such that designated areas should be reconsidered. I do not suggest that they should be abolished, on the contrary they should be extended; that is the scope of the legislation should be broadened because of certain factors. The Trois-Rivieres and Cap-de-la-Madeleine district is the centre of an urban area of 360,000 inhabitants where all those who are unemployed elsewhere in the area flock and try to find some work. I imagine that elsewhere in Canada, there are other similar urban areas which would deserve the consideration of the government with respect to tax incentives.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
On the other side of the municipality, in my own constituency there is Trois-Rivieres-Ouest which is part of the semi-rural section where a casern plant coming from California was to be established. They had bought the land and I believe that in the area where it would have been located, this would have been beneficial to everybody. Finally they decided to settle further off, in Louiseville. I am not exactly holding this against Louiseville, because I know it was needed there. But I find it strange that, for so short a distance, only 12 miles further, fiscal arrangements can be granted whereas they are refused 12 miles closer. This was a very serious American concern. Such legislation should probably be amended.
Mr. Chairman, what was called the Area Development Agency, if I understand correctly the report published by the Minister of Industry on the operations of the department

which was published, I think, last January 31, stipulated the following:
The Area Development Agency, which develops and administers programs to foster industrial growth in certain designated areas of Canada, has been organized into two main groups. One of these consists of area specialists who concentrate on particular regions of the country. These officers work with the operational branches of the department as well as with federal, provincial and municipal departments and organizations in promoting regional development. The other group administers the special incentives for designated areas.
I think we have reached the point where this Area Development Agency should not only be concerned with the designated areas but it should increase its co-operation with the Department of Industry, with the provincial departments and also the area representatives, and the industrial commissioners of the municipalities.
I believe that there should be closer contact. I have personally noticed that the Department of Industry can do all kinds of things, but neither our municipal councils nor our chambers of commerce are aware of it. In order to enable them to benefit fully, the scope of the operations of the Area Development Agency may have to be widened and their advertising increased.
Now, I am being rather brief because others want to participate in the discussion and I should not like to tax the patience of the committee. I spoke a while ago of the designated areas under the present legislation.
On moving industrial plants, something in Hansard caught my eye a few days ago. I see that it is not only back home that people complain about those things. In 1964, the mayor of Galt wrote a letter begging the government to prevent the act from being used to move existing industries within too limited an area. That, to a certain extent, is what I mean too.
Now, Mr. Chairman, before closing I would like to make another suggestion to the Minister of Industry. I would ask him to take it in the spirit in which I intend it. Looking over the literature I get from the Department of Industry, I note that out of, let us say, 30 high officials in the department, only three are French Canadian.
Far be it from me to want to play nationalist, jingoist or separatist, but in all frankness, and with all the serenity possible, I say that if we want to overcome the difficulties which are inflicted upon us and achieve mutual understanding between the two main ethnic groups, it might be wise to recruit more qualified French speaking staff for the upper
June 2, 1966

echelons in that department. Please note that I am not necessarily blaming the minister, I merely wish to make a constructive suggestion. It is not a question of removing the people who now hold those positions to give them to someone else, but rather one of recruiting qualified French Canadians when the time comes to fill vacancies. I did mention qualified people.
I know that it has been said in the past that we lacked qualified people; it has also been said that French Canadians were not anxious to join the civil service, but I believe that this time is now over. If qualified officials are needed in the department, it is surely possible to find some, so that within a reasonable time, without any rush, without dismissing anyone, in the group of 30 senior officials, we might find half a score of French Canadian names.
These are the constructive suggestions that I wanted to make. I will sum them up; Co-operation between the Department of Industry and municipal, industrial, provincial and regional agencies; review of the whole scope of the act concerning the designated areas policy; and extension of publicity concerning the activity of the area development agency.
Third and most constructive criticism: would it be possible to recruit more French speaking people for senior positions in this department as in others.
To conclude, I wish to congratulate once again the Minister of Industry, not only in my name, but also on the behalf of municipal councils and chambers of commerce who spoke of the fine job done by the minister for the past three years.

Mr. Chairman, I felt I would be derelict in my duty if I did not take advantage of the discussion on item No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Industry to support the proposition put forward this afternoon by my colleague, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, speaking on safety in motorcars. I have taken an interest in this subject for the past several years, particularly since a former Conservative member, Dr. Kucherepa, some years ago-I believe in the session of 1958-59-put some informative remarks on Hansard with respect to the problem of automobile safety.
My interest in this matter culminated in my placing Bill No. C-26 on the order paper on January 18, the subject matter of which has been referred to the standing committee
Supp ly-Industry
on justice and legal affairs. 1 take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi for having taken the initiative in bringing to public attention this very serious problem facing society today. I am sure it was gratifying to him that the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Northumberland supported his stand on the matter.
There is not too much I can say at the moment because I think the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi covered the subject matter very thoroughly, but it seems to me there is an inconsistency in the minds of the public with respect to safety, and particularly with respect to the various modes of transportation by air, water, rail, bus and automobile.
If there is a fatal air crash in which 50, 75 or 100 people are killed, immediately there is a great public outcry. We spend hundreds of thousands of dollars having our aeronautical boards, engineers and departments of government investigate to see if there was a mechanical defect. Air line officials themselves also carry out investigations. We also do the same thing if there is a disaster at sea. But every week end there are 50, 60 and some times 100 people killed in fatal accidents on the highways, and because they are killed on a helter-skelter, hit-or-miss basis all over the country the public does not express the same concern.
The first law of nature is self-preservation. Why should we not be just as concerned about fatal accidents on our highways as about accidents in the air or on the water? This is an important area for discussion. As time goes on I am sure public opinion will wholeheartedly support members like the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and others who have taken action on this matter.
It is heartening to see the lead taken by our friends across the border in the United States, particularly in the state of New York. It was interesting, after reading the latest reports of the U.S. Senate committee which is investigating this matter, to note that the chairman of that committee, when presenting a recommendation to the United States Senate, made reference to the fact that it was not only the nut behind the wheel but the nut in the wheel about which we should be concerned.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I think it can be said simply that there are three areas. There is the nut behind the wheel, as we so commonly refer to the man who may be reckless in his driving, there are

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
the roads themselves and the laws and regulations in respect of traffic on the highways, and then the vehicle itself. I think one reason more action has not been taken along the lines of what people have in mind is the fact that if one automobile company decides to introduce some safety measure this automatically involves a greater cost in bringing the vehicle to the public and as a consequence the vehicle is not quite as competitive. If we follow through with this new concept of considering the matter from a legal point of view and bringing in mandatory legislation with regard to safety devices on cars, automatically it will take in all vehicles sold by manufacturers in Canada or the United States and all cars imported into Canada. It would consequently make them competitive and we would thereby be removing the economic factor which apparently has been instrumental in retarding the advance of safety devices in automobiles.
I think such a move on the part of the government would be greatly welcomed by automobile manufacturers. If we were to take a definite stand I am sure this would be welcomed by the public and it would make the automobile manufacturers competitive. I should like to support what was said by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and the hon. member for Timiskaming to the effect that we should increase our budget of the Department of Industry and look into the matter of setting up some type of safety bureau or research centre in Canada which could make a thorough study of this problem. I am sure the government would receive widespread acclaim from the public if it were to take this action.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the representations which have been made this afternoon by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi who also appeared before the justice and legal affairs committee while it was studying the matter of auto safety. The hon. member made a most impressive and useful contribution. The hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Moose Mountain who also appeared before this committee made a very impressive and important contribution.
I wish to participate in this debate to ask the minister to give serious consideration to divesting himself of responsibility and authority in the whole field of automobile safety. I will come back to the urgency of automobile safety in a moment. I should like

to make the point right at the beginning, however, that as things stand now in the Department of Industry the minister is responsible for automobile safety and also at the same time is responsible for the administration and conduct of the United States-Canada auto parts agreement. As everybody knows, that agreement is dependent upon the good will and voluntary co-operation of the United States automobile industry.
The main effect of this is that the minister really is a captive of the United States automobile industry. In Canada, because of this agreement, we no longer have any control whatsoever over the automobile industry and the direction it is going to take. As a result of this the minister himself is, as I say, really a captive of the United States automobile industry. One of my friends says he is a prisoner. I would not go that far, but certainly he has a conflict of interest, I suggest, between the need to administer the new agreement and make it work and the need to act as a policeman in respect of the automobile industry in the area of safety itself. Consequently, if the minister is left with the responsibility of dealing with automobile safety I do not see how he can adequately fulfil this function, even with the best intentions in the world. I do not say that he would deliberately neglect it, but I think the more one examines his department and the auto industry, the more one is impressed by the fact that he simply will not be able to be a captive of the United States auto industry on the one hand and try to act as a policeman in the field of auto safety on the other hand.
I know all ministers are empire builders and are reluctant to divest themselves of certain areas of authority and jurisdiction. However, if the minister really is anxious, as I am sure he is, to deal with the problem of automobile safety, I think he should consider seriously passing over authority in this field from himself to perhaps the Solicitor General, the Minister of Justice or anyone else except the Minister of Industry because, as I have said, I think as we proceed we will find that he simply will not be able to act as a policeman in the auto industry at the same time that he is going to go to the industry to seek its co-operation and big-hearted help in making the auto parts agreement an effective instrument in our economy and in the automotive industry of Canada. I suggest very seriously that the minister give this point consideration.
June 2, 1366

The other matter, which probably has been raised by other members while 1 was not in the chamber, is a mandatory scheme of automobile safety. Already in our examination of the subject it is becoming increasingly apparent that we should have a mandatory scheme, not only from the point of view of the public but also from the point of view of the manufacturers as well. Any information we have been able to obtain so far indicates that if you have a voluntary automobile scheme it will be a failure. Experience in the United States has indicated that the automotive industry itself, because of its competitive nature, will not and cannot adhere to a voluntary scheme of automobile safety. Unless you bring in a mandatory scheme which puts all the automobile companies on the same basis and forces all automobile companies to put the same safety features in their cars, it seems to me you will not have a scheme which will be successful. Because they all are so competitive with each other, not one of them will do it, and even if one should do it the others will shortcircuit it in order to obtain a competitive price advantage.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The automobile people themselves are now coming to the conclusion that the most effective system of safety standards would be a mandatory one requiring all automobiles to have the same number of safety features. I doubt whether the public yet realizes just what an enormous problem this constitutes in our country. The tragedy is that it is one which is capable of solution. No doubt it already has been pointed out that in the past ten years over 35,000 people have been killed in automobile accidents in Canada and 948,000 have been injured. By the end of this year almost, 5,000 people will die and another 150,000 will be injured. Between 1966 and the end of 1970 26,000 Canadians will die on our roads and more than one million people will be injured. Automobile accidents are now the leading cause of death and injury in this as in many countries. It is estimated that about half of all our cars are going to be involved sooner or later in injury producing accidents. The cost to the public in terms of lost income, personal suffering and accident claims amounts to a fantastic and staggering total.
As I said earlier, studies have already shown that the whole problem of automobile safety confronting this country is of the first magnitude. We have all been following the investigations taking place in the United States which have pinpointed even more
Supply-Industry
dramatically the problem that has been created. It has been said that a good many deaths and injuries and a good deal of suffering can be prevented. For example, 87 per cent of all traffic accidents and 45 per cent of highway fatalities occur at speeds of less than 40 miles per hour. It is commonly thought that the real problem in this regard relates to high speed, cars roaring along the highway, but that is not true. The major killer and producer of injuries is the car travelling at less than 40 miles per hour.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi has documented this situation on various occasions both inside and outside the house and has shown that the real causes of accidents and deaths can be related to instrument panels, steering assemblies, faulty windshields, door structures and the lack of headrests on seats. These are all items involving safety features which could be made mandatory, and the total cost of installing them in cars on an assembly line basis is estimated at between $100 and $150 per car. In spite of this, we in this country seem prepared to sit silently by and permit this carnage to continue year after year, resulting in high insurance premiums, deaths, injuries, suffering and heartache to the people of Canada.
It is not necessary for us to document this whole situation in more detail at this stage. I am sure the minister is familiar with the statistics, and in view of the representations he has received I am sure he is about to rise and announce a strong program for his department in relation to this whole matter. In order that he will have an opportunity to do so I will now sit down.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I must say a few words about Canadian industry, its financing, and the sale and marketing of its products. This is the subject I would like to deal with in the house.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the aim of industry is to manufacture and sell as much as possible; to manufacture as much as possible with the least effort. In Canada, as in many other countries, we have this facility of manufacturing many products by automation, employing scarcely any manpower.
I could mention the case of an industry which I know very well, which employed 800 people some ten years ago whereas now there are only about a hundred, although production has increased tenfold.

June 2. 1866
Supply-Industry
This is the result of automation, which is right here before us and which we must face. This is what I would like to talk about: automation and industry.
Since automation, that is science or technology, is replacing man, will we use more manpower to help develop industry, or shall we create a new industry with new technical means? One must not be against development and automation, but I must say we cannot create employment and give everyone work in Canadian industry, because the aim of the latter is not to create employment but to meet the demand. This is the aim of industry, which has certainly understood its purpose. It has reached its goal.
Now we must face the problem of manpower. People most earn their living, they must accept industry.
We have designated areas in Canada where there is a shortage of manpower. Again, I could mention the case of an industry which pays about $1,500 a week in salaries and manufactures $10,000 worth of products. Do you think $1,500 can buy for $10,000? I put this question to the hon. minister, and I think he will be able to answer it. This is the state of the economy across Canada.
With regard to our designated areas, we want to develop industry in every way. Concerning industry, Canada has created various bodies to help industry, such as AR-DA or IDA, as it is called, which I believe can help industry independently of the provinces.
We know that ARDA is the body concerned with joint programs and that all those programs must be submitted and accepted by the provinces, after which the federal government contributes to a certain extent to the development of industry.
In connection with the industrial areas where it is desired to set up and extend industries, the first question which comes to my mind is the following: are goods lacking in Canada? Does industry manufacture enough goods to meet the needs of the Canadian people? I would say yes, because we now have industrial surpluses which have been accumulating for approximately 15 years and cannot be marketed.
I know that there may be a shortage of goods in various industrial sectors. For instance, in the steel industry, there might be a shortage of steel; it is perhaps not being produced in sufficient quantities, but it is our duty to build steel works so as to produce

enough steel. It is our duty and it is the duty of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury).
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
There is no shortage of goods in Canada. In 1965, for instance, statistics indicate that from $51 to $52 billion of goods were produced, of which $35 billion were marketed, exported and sold. The balance is in warehouses, on shelves and remain unsold. It is up to the Minister of Industry to increase production and develop industry. He must also look after the consumption and the sale of those goods. This may not come exclusively under the Minister of Industry, but other departments are concerned. On the other hand, I feel it is the duty of all ministers and citizens of Canada to look sifter the distribution of goods, and to see to it that goods are sold according to the needs of the Canadian people.
We have a great number of citizens in this country who manage to reach a certain degree of affluence, who manage to buy products by means of loans. They profit by progress and science on credit, by borrowing money. We want to develop industry in designated areas, but we find that industrialists have no money and the governments have to guarantee their loans to assist industry.
I am not against assisting industry. If consumers had money to pay, we could do without all those socialist regulations and plans which bog down citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I know several industries in those designated areas, which want to expand and could do so. There are industrialists who were born in parishes or in certain areas where they like to live, but they cannot expand their industries under the present system. Under the new program of the Department of Industry, industries are granted 10 per cent for expansion and construction purposes. If an industry moves to another area, it becomes a new industry and can get one third of construction and equipment costs. Why not grant one third to existing industries which want to expand but cannot do so by themselves.
There are always restrictions and conditions which result in a very small number of industries and companies being able to avail themselves of the advantages afforded by the government. If advantages are offered let them be such that people can avail themselves of them.
Why do industries lack money? Why do industries no longer find capital in Canada?
June 2, 1366

It is precisely because the federal, provincial and municipal governments, the school boards and the church councils get what little savings may exist in Canada, and when one wants to develop an industry, there is no money, no capital left.
The government has absorbed all the capital by way of taxes and debentures. Thus, Canadians and industries are deprived of their assets to the point that several industries can no longer operate without getting into debt. Almost all industries are financed. A large number of them can operate only thanks to the Industrial Bank, which can be of great service but not to every one, because its interests are too high and its reimbursement period is too short. For short term reimbursement, you have to make profits to pay back the Industrial Bank. But when you make profits, you must pay taxes which, added to the reimbursements, put you in an almost impossible situation. So, many industrialists and businessmen are unable to borrow because taxes are too heavy, the reimbursement period is too short and interest rates are too high.
I would ask the Minister of Industry to take a look into the Industrial Bank to see if there would not be a way of extending the reimbursement period. There should be loans payable in 20 years. Seven or ten years is not long enough to reimburse $300,000 to $500,000. It is impossible to do so.
I think the minister has already realized it. He has all the facts before him. I know he is aware that many industries cannot operate because those interest rates are too high. They cannot sell their products because the consumer cannot buy them, having no money left after paying too many taxes and too much interest. All Canadians lie at the mercy of the government. They cannot meet their own needs because they have no money. When governments put money into circulation, they come and get more than we have. The situation is getting more confused all the time. That is not the way to solve the problem.
If we want to settle the problem of industry in Canada, Mr. Chairman, we will have to take the required steps. Industry is on the same footing in the province of Quebec as everywhere else in Canada. The industrialist has had more advantages then the farmer and yet it had to run into more debt. Industrial debts are enormous. All these financial interests, all these taxes contribute to increase the cost of living and to create 23033-373
Supply-Industry
inflation in Canada. Inflation is due to the unbalanced system we have. That system must be balanced. If there are in Canada a hundred million products for sale, there should be as much money in the hands of our citizens to buy those products. It is just the opposite our government and the economy gave the Canadian people.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
This cannot go on in the same way forever. Even though new industries are being developed, these will not go far if they cannot sell their products. And they will not be able to sell them because wages they pay are not high enough to allow people to buy their production.
Then, we will have to give dividends or discounts compensated on prices. These dividends or compensated discounts should be granted by the Bank of Canada, the official body that can also be used to create capital and to put into circulation the required money in order to create the buying power needed so that our products are in good demand in Canada.
We can rely on different countries to sell our products, but everybody knows that when you export to other countries you have to import for just about the same amount. Thus, international trade does not make much difference, as far as production by the people of Canada is concerned. There has to be Canadian purchasing power in the hands of Canadians, in order to sell Canadian products.
Such are the solutions the minister should suggest to the government. If some others have found other remedies, they should be brought forward. Nobody has yet been able to find means of solving our economic problems, so as to solve the distribution problem.
There are almost no problems as far as production is concerned. All the minister has to do is to ask for the production he needs and I can assure you that he will get it.
I can tell you that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is telling us, for instance, that production is at a maximum in Canada, that it is almost impossible to produce more, I say this is not true. The Minister of Finance talks nonsense when saying such things, because I know a large number of industries which could double their production in a few days, in a few months. Then comes the question of labour: well, we have all those people busy on winter works, which are

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
useless. That kind of work doesn't give anything, it is wasting the people's money.
If those people were employed in industry, they would be working for Canada and producing something. Many citizens are on social welfare, but I am told that the moment they begin to work, they lose their social benefits. These people could produce something but, as it is, they are not.
Canada's productive force totals seven million people, of which approximately three million are not earning enough money to pay income tax. This means that those Canadians are not working very long nor very often. It also means that they could produce ten times more. There are strikes throughout Canada, people curtailing production; all those problems could be solved and the hon. minister would have many things to do in that field. I am not putting all the blame on him, as he is not the one who invented the present system, but he is not doing much to set it right. The present system is not working anymore, it is fundamentally obsolete; it is working only for those who are controlling money and credit, in brief, it is adding to the wealth of those who are controlling money and credit and to the impoverishment of the rest of the population.
This is why strikes happen; people are altogether too poor.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to tell the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac that he is wasting his time, and I wish he wouldn't. Now, it is not incumbent upon me to settle his problems; perhaps he had better direct his speech to my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp).

Mr. Chairman, I may reply to the minister that if I am wasting my time, he is also wasting his, for he does nothing to improve the situation.
If there is need to talk to the Minister of Finance, let the Minister of Industry do it, for he is in a better position than I; besides, it is his duty.
So, Mr. Chairman, there are still many things I could say, but I believe I have spoken of the main ones. I feel that if we seek mutual understanding, if we really want to serve the Canadian nation and the industry itself, we could find the necessary means, and use those which are at our disposal, to settle the various problems that beset industry, production and consumption.
There are two problems, production and consumption. The main one is consumption,
[Mr. Latulippe.l
since production is not lacking at the present time. I am not against new industries, on the contrary, I want them to be created, but I wonder how long they could operate, or sell their products, if consumption cannot be financed.
We have accepted technique, science and progress in all fields, but we should especially welcome technique, science and progress in the economic field on a national scale.

Mr. Chairman, I would like for a few moments to discuss the estimates, but not along the same lines as the member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe) because in spite of the little knowledge I may have, I do not know how he came to the somewhat eccentric ideas he attempted to outline, which, in my opinion, one could not make head or tail of, and which did not relate at all to the estimates of the Department of Industry.
You have heads and tails; what solution have you found? People are starving.

I would like, Mr. Chairman, to draw the attention of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) on a special point concerning my riding. It is a problem which, I know, now holds the attention of the minister and, especially, that of many voters in my riding. It concerns the Valcartier arsenal which, since about 25 years, served to the production of ammunitions for the Canadian government, and which the Department of Defence Production decided, two years ago, to sell to private enterprise; the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) is especially interested in it since this is an attempt, I submit respectfully, to create, within private enterprise, an important industry which will have for effect, not to decrease but to increase employment and the number of employees which, unfortunately, have been decreasing there for a few years.
The Valcartier arsenals have been producing ammunitions for more than 20 years and required at certain times the services of at least 3,000 male and female employees. There are now only about 350 employees in Valcartier and many of these plants are not operating, precisely because it is not necessary that they operate to full capacity to carry out contracts with the Department of Defence Production.
Now, as a whole, even if the staff now working in that plant has some apprehension
June 2, 1966

concerning the sale of this industry to private enterprise, I think they should understand that if the industry is sold to private enterprise, the whole industry will be able to manufacture, in addition to ammunitions, other things which could compete with the general civil production with which, we must admit, it is impossible for the government to compete.
I respectfully submit that the Minister of Industry, in his forthcoming dealings, should point out to the buyers the importance of respecting the vested rights of present employees.
I am convinced that the rights of the present employees being respected, the buyers will not only be in a position to keep the present employees at the Valcartier arsenal, but in a near future, they will rehire from 2,000 to 3,000 employees to reach their previous strength, because precisely a great number of those mills could be used for civil production where the Canadian government cannot compete against private enterprise.
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Industry for the conscientious work he has been doing in that field for some time.
I, for one, am convinced that this decision will be welcomed by the general public, and that the acquirers will thus be able to get a maximum production out of this war plant which can thereby be changed into a peace plant.
I also think that, generally speaking, the department acted wisely in adjudicating the production of ammunition to private enterprise, so that it could bet the lowest possible competitive price.

Mr. Chairman, I can well imagine the minister being a bit impatient and I do not blame him.
There are two things I wish to mention. In my district quite large quantities of excellent birch are being destroyed. I can think of one instance of nearly a million feet of lumber being cut for which there is no market. The local people have made several efforts to see if they could not establish a furniture factory in the district to utilize this and other very suitable woods for the manufacture of furniture. I should like to direct the minister's attention to this matter and to ask him if he can do anything about it. I should also like to ask him to provide some information in this regard to the persons interested.

There is another matter which I mentioned to him privately, a few days ago, can the minister tell me whether any research has been done with respect to the small chippers for chipping culled logs so that they can be sent to the pulp mills? At the present time machinery is available to do this but it is much too expensive for the ordinary tree farmer or small operator. Will the minister look into the situation and see if something can be done to provide this type of machinery on a smaller scale than that at present provided to the large industries? With these few remarks I shall take my seat.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very grateful indeed for the remarks, or most of them, which have been made during the course of this discussion. I appreciate some of the flattering comments and I am particularly grateful for the number of suggestions that have been made for the future guidance of the department in the execution of its programs.
This is a new department and, I suppose, in terms of government it is very new indeed. Neither the officials nor myself are persuaded that all the answers have yet been found, but we are looking for them and consequently we appreciate new ideas. This does not mean that we shall accept all suggestions, but at least we shall look at them.
One general question asked by the hon. member for Villeneuve respecting the Department of Industry was: How is it that Canadians appear able to afford, as outlined in the estimate book, the sum of $25 million for defence development but only a very much smaller sum indeed for civilian development? At page 178 of the blue book of estimates this item appears under vote No. 5:
To sustain technological capability in Canadian industry by supporting the selected defence development programs . . . $25,000,000.
Under vote 10 the following appears:
To advance the technological capability of Canadian manufacturing industry by supporting selected civil (non-defence) development . . . $8,770,000.
This does not in any way indicate a greater predeliction or preoccupation with defence equipment development in industry as opposed to civil development. The problem that exists with relation to the support of development projects in defence industry has been in existence for a considerable number of years and consequently more people are familiar

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
with it. Some people are in a position to take advantage of it successfully, and the department is more capable of effectively administering it.
Vote 10 has to do with a new program which, for practical purposes, is entering its second full year. While last year there was provided in relation to the operation of this program the sum of $5 million, the figure is now $8,770,000. We expect that as this program acquires public acceptance, that is, by the manufacturing public, and as the department acquires more skill in administration, the amounts set for the support of advancement of technology in the civil field will grow. The necessity of growth in the military field is not quite so apparent.
In relation to the department two other major items were mentioned. One was the area development program, and its operation, and the other was the automobile safety program. I might deal with the second program first.
I should like to felicitate the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi for the very excellent work he has done and is doing in bringing home to the Canadian public the extent to which this is a problem in Canada and for making clear that statistically, in relative terms, what he talks of is a greater problem here than in the United States. He has done a very valuable service in bringing this problem to public attention and directing public attention to it. The government for its part, and I happen to be its spokesman on this subject for the moment, is undertaking to provide some practical and acceptable solutions to the problem.
The first step in providing suitable solutions to any problem is to find out what the problem is and what is known about it. Then you must organize all information. When you have a background of information you then endeavour to bring intellectual effort to bear on the problem in the hope that a solution can be worked out co-operatively in the best interests of all concerned.
I am glad to say that the National Research Council has just completed a review of current knowledge in this particular field relating to what has been somewhat disparagingly called the nut behind the wheel, the nut on the wheel and, finally, the place where the nut falls off the wheel, which is the road, under these three headings nine technical reports have been issued by the National Research Council. Should any hon. member be interested in them I should be only too it.

delighted to make all nine volumes available to him. These volumes contain a very valuable summary of the current state of knowledge in this field and provide an indispensable background for anyone trying to find effective solutions to the problem.
For its part the government, in co-operation with the Traffic Accident Research Foundation and the Canadian Highway Safety Council, has commissioned a draft automobile safety code, as it has been so far called, which will be submitted to the scrutiny of a conference to be held in June. Members at the conference will examine the draft code on the strength of the reports providing basic information about the driver, the car and the environment on the road. This conference will be composed of representatives of federal and provincial authorities concerned with highway safety, also of various private and semi-private organizations in Canada concerned with traffic safety and, finally, some other individuals who have demonstrated an interest in safety. There will be an expose of the problem at this meeting. There will be suggested parameters which it is hoped the conference will accept. If they are accepted steps will be taken to try to bring them into force.
Referring to what was said by the hon. member for Timiskaming, who in a way indicated the nature of the problem, I may say that we have in this country a number of statutory speed limits. One would assume that a safe car should be designed for travelling at those speeds. Owing, no doubt, to special circumstances involving time, some drivers, as indicated by the hon. member for Timiskaming, do not pay attention to those speed limits. Therefore it is clearly not possible to design cars from the safety point of view to be driven within the statutory speed limits, because there will be people who will pay no attention to such statutory limits. Clearly it is not enough to provide the safety devices in cars that he suggests. The mere provision of those will have no effect if they are not used. The hon. member has indicated that although he has incorporated a shoulder harness in his car he has never had occasion to use it. As I recollect, his son used it after he had turned the car over. I do not think anybody would deliberately turn a car over. That should not be a prerequisite of or a prelude to using a safety harness.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had indicated some views on the question of automobile safety, and had stated that in terms of focus for federal government action the Department of Industry was not the most appropriate department. Consideration is being given

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
to what would be a more appropriate department to look after this.
A question was asked whether more money is needed to get an automobile safety program under way. I do not think at the present moment that shortage of funds is in any way hindering what has to be done, namely the acquisition and organization of information, and the development of a program after having sorted out the various jurisdictions. I think we are taking productive steps to organize the information, to get agreement on jurisdictions and to launch a program. The government is seized of the importance of this particular problem facing Canada today to at least as great an extent as other hon. members.
The next item examined was the area development program, and observations respecting it were to some degree contradictory. This would indicate to me that a program, which those who find themselves outside of designated areas desire to have abolished, and those who are alongside designated areas seek to have extended to them, is a useful and successful one.
However, I should point out in respect of a number of the representations which were made that there is a fundamental basis to this whole concept. It is a measure in an area in which the federal government has jurisdiction, namely the field of unemployment, and the program is one designed to bring some measure of relief to areas suffering from high chronic unemployment.
We measure this unemployment in two ways as accurately as we can. The first is through registrations under the national employment service. Where the number of registrations in an N.E.S. area rises above a certain figure, or is above a certain figure for a sustained period in relation to the total labour force in that area, then automatically the area qualifies for the incentive benefits.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speechtext:
The functions of the area development agency as a whole relate to industrial development and area development, but the designated area program is limited to being a program related to unemployment. One of the reasons for this is that under our constitution the provinces regard economic

development, and the determination of priorities for economic development within a province, as being a matter for the provinces not for the federal government. If there were to be a move into this particular field, an attempt on the part of the federal government to set priorities for economic development, this would be a matter of concurrent jurisdiction with the provinces, administered as is the ARDA program.
The ARDA program is for the purpose of encouraging economic development of rural areas within a province. Hon. members will recall that under it the initiatives for programs within a specific area are taken by the province, not by the federal government; and the criteria are determined by the province, not by the federal government. This is in a sense the classic shared-cost program, in which the determination of criteria and the administration of the program rest with the province, or provinces, and the role of the federal government is largely confined to assisting in financing the projects.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext: Can industrial plants be built under that scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Industrial plants can be built under ARDA. There is no limitation in respect of the purposes or objects for which ARDA funds are used. I think this is a useful and interesting distinction. It indicates first the nature of the constitutional problem and why this particular incentive program is based on unemployment. Whether based on national employment service registrations or on areas where the national employment service registry is an accurate index, recourse to unemployment figures is an aid in considering the average level of non-farm family income.
I was asked by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek where the statistics with regard to non-farm family income were derived. The statistics were obtained from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and their definition of a non-farm family is accepted for the purposes of those statistics. Non-farm family income is used, because in cases where the non-farm family income is very low there is an assumption that even though within the family there may be people who are unemployed but not registered, the numbers involved will depress the average non-farm family income, and consequently in this way indicate to some degree, where there are not
June 2, 1966

accurate national employment service registrations, the level of unemployment or underemployment. That is the reason this is used.
The purpose of this program is not to raise the family income level; it is to relieve unemployment. The income figures were used and spoken of lightly as another way of measuring unemployment or underemployment. If this is understood, it is quite clear that one cannot take into account, as any criteria or as any basis for the program, other economic factors such as rate of economic growth, slowness of economic growth, or indeed rate of population growth or lack of it. All these are measures of economic growth of an area and, as I say, the determination of priorities in respect of economic growth within a province is something which the provinces control, and which under their constitution they regard properly as being within their competence and jurisdiction, and not under federal jurisdiction.
A number of members from the maritime provinces have represented that in order to make this an effective program to stimulate economic growth, there should be designated the metropolitan areas in the maritimes, notably Halifax, Dartmouth, Fredericton and Saint John. Even though unemployment was at a very low level both in regional and national terms in these metropolitan areas, to designate these areas, on the grounds that these areas currently of low unemployment are at a disadvantage in relation to other areas in the maritimes with higher employment, would mean that the deliberate advantage conferred on areas of high unemployment with a view to alleviating this would disappear. The program having as its basis the bringing of jobs to those who are without work would fail completely.
Recognizing that in some areas the incentive program will not be the answer and will not effectively reduce unemployment, if it exists there, members will be aware that the government has made available to the individual an alternative program, should he wish to make use of it, which would provide assistance to persons without work to move from the area in which they or their families are to an area where there will be job opportunities. These two approaches are not conflicting; they merely supplement one another and provide a desirable choice to areas which have some high unemployment.
There was some representation by members from some of the westerly areas that
Supply-Industry
comparisons of designated areas with smaller areas not too far geographically removed from them appeared to disclose that conditions inside the designated area, and just outside, were substantially similar. This of course would be expected because it is rather rare that one finds an area of high economic activity and low unemployment, and then just right across some invisible boundary line an area of high unemployment and low economic activity.
These changes tend to occur rather gradually in geographic terms, and in moving from an area of high economic activity and low unemployment to an area of low economic activity and high unemployment there will not be a corridor; as one proceeds in distance there will be a merging or a gradual transition from the first condition to the second. So, wherever the line is drawn, conditions immediately adjacent to that line and on either side of it will be substantially similar. Obviously the line has to be drawn somewhere, unless the whole country is to be designated. Obviously right adjacent to the line there will, understandably, be feelings of invidiousness in that the man on the favourable side of the line has an advantage which his almost neighbour just across the line does not enjoy, although the neighbour feels the conditions where he finds himself are substantially the same-and indeed they are.
The criteria for the delineation of these areas has been the national employment service areas, largely for the following reasons. In their present configurations they are supposed to represent areas of homogeneous economic activity; each is supposed to be an economic unit. Second, over a number of years there have been gathered for these areas, on an area basis, the kind of statistics on which we have to rely. Indeed these are the only records we have on which to determine which area qualifies for designation and which does not. If one is to operate a program based on objective measurable criteria and standards, he must rely on statistical evidence which has been gathered over a period of time. I accept the difficulty there is in comparing conditions close to and on either side of a line of demarcation, but I do not know of any way to avoid them.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
We are continually receiving representations as to the appropriateness of the N.E.S. areas, and I heard some new ones in the current debate. These are reviewed as the

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
representations are made and periodically, following discussions with the soon to-be department of manpower, which will be responsible for the operation of the national employment service, changes are made in the boundaries of the N.E.S. areas where it appears that the existing boundaries produce social inequalities or social injustice. This forms part of the periodic review which is carried out in respect of the qualification of N.E.S. areas for designation or de-designation.
I think I indicated in my opening statement that this program had to date been a very successful one. In order to provide incentives, one must offer advantages to a limited number of people; and the more limited the number of people, the more effective are the incentives. These incentives are now offered to areas of Canada comprising some 15 per cent of the total Canadian labour force. If, as has been suggested by some members-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production

speechtext: Just a moment. To the best of my knowledge, Haliburton has had a number of forest products industries. I presume this takes in the sawmill, as well as various resort areas where there would be seasonal unemployment. But conditions in Haliburton today are not much worse than they have been for the last 30 years. They probably have not changed very much in 30 years. There is no acute problem in th:s area; it is a problem of a chronic nature
I turn now to Manitoulin island. Manitoulin island, it seems to me, cannot be considered as being an industrial area. In my opinion the people on the island are not much interested in its becoming an industrial area. I know there are hon. members listening to me who have hunted and fished on the island, and chased deer all round it. They are aware that this is primarily an agricultural area. I believe the Prime Minister can rest assured that when the price of turkeys goes up everyone on the island will be very happy about the situation around Christmas time and Thanksgiving. I doubt whether one would find a serious unemployment picture on Manitoulin island, if one thinks of unemployment in terms of the national unemployment figures as they are usually compiled.
In my opinion these are not the kinds of definitions which fit into the criteria about which the minister has been speaking. Incidentally let me say there are more good people working in the hon. gentleman's department than most people realize. Indeed there is a superfluity of people. He has people there who are probably more frustrated than civil servants in other departments, because their efforts are not being utilized to any degree. These people joined the department to help decentralize industry and provide industrial equality across Canada. But they find this is not being done. It is not being done in Ontario, either, because of the inactivity of the department of economic planning under Mr. Randall. He, like his
Supply-Industry
predecessor, has paid more attention to manufacturing, to sales and to the propaganda side of his department than to the economic development which we believe must take place.
Again, in this department of economic planning there are some very good people. The province has been divided into areas and most of these areas have economic planning agencies. In my own area we have the Northeastern Ontario Development Association. The provincial government is allotting funds to these agencies and these are the agencies which are able to assist the federal government in its economic development projects. I am sure the minister's officials will tell him that co-operation with these agencies is essential if the program he is putting forward is to be anything more than window dressing.
The minister has said it is not wise to extend the boundaries too widely. Can he tell me why all the districts of northern Ontario should not be designated, without interfering with anything being done in connection with other programs? If this were done, areas which have the necessary natural resources would be able to take advantage of industries which are already contemplating expansion.
In my own area the firm of E. B. Eddy will be forced to go into the pulp and paper industry at Elk Lake within the next two years or they will lose their limits. They say it is difficult to raise capital amounting to $45 millions, and they may be right. A program of this kind will assist the company to come into an area where they have limits which they can operate for 30 or 40 years before the expiry date.
Work could be done to develop a chip industry in connection with the pulp and paper process and this would use up a great deal of what are now waste products. These things could happen if leadership were given by the department. But if the minister thinks he can operate this program in isolation, controlling from the top the development of particular industries in the areas he designates, he is under an illusion. He will not be able to get along without the co-operation of the provinces.
I do not know what we can do about this. Last year I decided to carry on a filibuster and I have no objection to doing so again. But it is unfair, and the responsibility must rest solely on the shoulders of the minister if some of the estimates of other government departments do not come up for discussion. I am hesitant to take this course, not because I

June 2. 1966
Supply-Industry
do not think it is possible, but because I do not think we have the right to do it. Surely there is some other way of calling attention to this problem without embarking on a full-fledged filibuster, until everyone is willing to tear their hair.
The minister is a reasonable man. He knows how these things work. He must be aware of the position in his own caucus. He knows that almost everybody in Canada agrees that he should help these areas of slow growth. If they are not getting their fair share of the benefits of the national economy, something should be done to help them.
In my own area there is literally no unemployment. This does not mean we have jobs at Kirkland Lake or that there are as many people in employment as was formerly the case. It means that people get into their cars and drive to Toronto. We have a high school at Kirkland Lake which has 1,200 students. The new Lisgar high school has 900. We have big vocational schools in Kirkland Lake and New Liskeard but almost none of the people we train can find jobs in the area, and so they go to Toronto. My son in Toronto tells me that any time he wants to have a party, within two hours he can contact 100 people from his home area who are living in the city. There are probably 4,000 to 5,000 people in Toronto who should be able to get work in their home area. This is a problem we damned well are going to solve. We are not going to move all our young people out of their home area. As a nation we do not want to see our people move to the United States.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
People move from northern Ontario to southern Ontario simply because the Minister of Industry has not been able to plan development along two simple lines. I ask him to point out any industry he has located in a designated area which does not meet two criteria. Either a man from the area got a bright idea and started a factory with his own money or, alternatively, a firm moved into the area because the raw materials were to be found in it.
In one election I argued that we would have to force industry into northern Ontario. Everybody threw up their hands at my suggestion, but within the last several weeks the minister heard delegates from a number of cities in northern Ontario use the word "force" in connection with the location of industry in that area.
Certainly the minister must provide a carrot. There is a $10 million item provided, but

all he expects to spend on this program in 1965-6 is $300,000. That is how successful the plan is. It is not working; it has not worked. The minister should take this problem to a committee where decisions could be made on the type of program that will provide the necessary development.
One problem in attracting industry to our area is that Mrs. Jones, wife of the superintendent of the plant contacted, wants to shop at Eaton's in Toronto and go to the O'Keefe Centre. Her husband likes to play golf at Runnymede golf course, or whatever the name may be. The manpower department will have to do something about such a problem and point out some of the advantages in northern Ontario, where those who like to do so can ski for six months of the year-although that does not overcome the golfing problem.
Everyone agrees that we want diversification of industry. Building factories on top of factories in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver is not always to the advantage of the nation. Hon. members from the west who are not participating in this debate because it concerns industry will soon face the problem that we have in northern Ontario, with more and more of their people moving into cities and leaving the farms. They are not able to find work down the street or in the next small village. They move to other provinces. I ask, does everybody in Manitoba finally wind up in Winnipeg? Does everybody in Saskatchewan end up in Regina? Does everybody in Alberta end up in Edmonton?
The representatives in Toronto are equally silent on this problem. They just do not believe there is anything but southern Ontario. Occasionally they may take a trip to northern Ontario to fish, but that is about all. The criteria we established are not working.
