The minister really does not understand the criteria. This is not a program similar to ARDA. ARDA is not going to build industries and factories, although some limited industrial development can take place under it. It is not an adjunct to this program.
I agree pressure was put on the minister to have this go to a committee where the criteria could be discussed, but he has not seen fit to let that happen. If he wants me to agree to the passing of his estimates I would still be willing to take his word, if he says he will send the criteria and designations to a committee, as he agreed to do last June. If not, I am going to discuss each individual case because I want to know what happened and why it did not work.
I have lots of time, Mr. Chairman. Maybe the minister's colleagues and some other hon. members do not, but this matter is important not only to me but to all hon. members who live in the northern parts of Canada. This applies to northern Quebec, and Quebec members should take a look at the situation because, as the hon. member for Villeneuve said the other day, this problem is as acute in his areas as it is in mine. I am sure the same is true in northern Manitoba, northern Alberta, northern Saskatchewan and northern B.C., to say nothing of the maritime provinces.
I think the hon. member for Danforth was right when he said there is a great deal of misunderstanding between the province of Ontario and the federal government. I was of the opinion that the minister had personnel working in co-operation with the Ontario government on economic development, but if this is not true I will be surprised.
Maybe when the minister returns to the chamber tomorrow he will be able to indicate what developments have taken place since last summer in Bracebridge, Collingwood, Parry Sound, Elliot Lake and Sturgeon Falls and, if he wants to, he can throw in Manitoulin island, which I consider to be an interloper on this particular matter.
A considerable change has been made in this program. The minister should read the Throne Speech in which it was indicated that this program was to help slow growth areas of Canada, and equalize opportunities for employment for all the people of Canada. That was the election promise which was made in most of the non-urban ridings in Ontario during the last federal election.
We are anxious to understand this program and we are trying as hard as possible to

June 2, 1966
Supply-Industry
persuade the minister to be open minded about making a change, because the plan is not working in the areas that need it most. I would like to know what has happened in the province of Quebec in places like Aylmer, Gaspe and Maniwaki, and in Mont Laurier, which is not far from here, and in Matane and Megantic. These are small communities which are not in a similar position to places like Chatham, Windsor, Wallaceburg; or a place such as Cornwall, which is situated on the St. Lawrence seaway and able to take advantage of the development of the seaway. There is a considerable difference between these communities.
If this is a good plan I would like to know what objection there is to changing the criteria. I may be wrong about the amount the department has put into it, but if I read the estimates correctly, total expenditure under the statutory provision for incentives for development of industrial employment opportunities in designated areas is to be $300,000, which is not much out of a $10 million program.
If that is all we are spending out of a $10 million program, can the minister give me any good reason why we should not extend the program to other areas that are not covered by it? Personally I cannot see why he is reluctant to do this or to consider it.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
If we have the money and if the government is interested in developing secondary industry in areas where there is a slow growth situation, we should be prepared at least to set up a relationship with the provincial government to see what can be mutually worked out between the two to spend some of the $10 million we are providing. I do not know whether or not the minister knows off hand what industries are developing in Bracebridge, or whether there is going to be any development in Collingwood or some of the other communities. It would not be difficult for me to take a drive over to check. I think I could phone Toronto and find out from one of the area development agencies in Ontario whether or not there has been any talk. It always is very interesting to find, in speaking to members of the department, that the interest they have is exactly the same as that being expressed, for instance, in my area, in the Northeastern Development Association. If somebody is talking about a new plant coming in, everybody is talking about it and taking a certain amount of credit for it. So it would seem to me there is a

certain amount of overlapping and some cooperation between the various departments in that regard. For that reason I believe the minister should be in a position to give us this kind of information.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I really do not know what can be accomplished by this. I should like the minister to fulfil the promise he made to the house and send both the criteria and the designated area program to the committee. Previously he agreed to do this. Really I do not see why he disagrees now. I do not see why he would not rather do that than discuss some of these criteria in the house tomorrow. I am sure some of the officials would be quite prepared to take credit for the work they have done, and give an indication of the fields of endeavour which they intend to pursue. I am sure that then the members of the house might be in a position to decide whether or not the criteria are satisfactory to them. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, it is neither satisfactory to me nor to the area which I represent. This is well known. It has been well known for some time. The minister, unimpeachable as he may be with his long association with the Department of Defence Production, where they really do not have to answer to anyone, because it is a highly complex field, is perhaps finding it difficult to associate with some of the other persons who have gone into this criteria, and who have not found it is as simple a proposition as the minister has indicated.
Two years ago I had the opportunity to sit in with a number of the officials of the Department of Labour. At that time officials were brought in from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. They discussed the criteria being used at that time and there were new criteria. The criteria about which we were particularly concerned were those which would provide for an increase in the economic growth in those areas where population is decreasing because of the lack of primary industry, particularly those industries that suffered a gradual decline before the five year period which is in the criteria now. I should like to use the example of Kirkland Lake. From 1937 to 1939 Kirkland Lake hit its peak of employment. Following the war it decreased because activities stopped in some of the gold mines in that area. As the mines closed down the population decreased. The population did not fit into the criteria, for the simple reason that those who were over age 50 had worked underground for 30 years and
June 2, 1966	COMMONS
found it impossible to retrain for any type of employment. In addition they had homes in that area, had raised their children there, and had friends there. At that time most of them retired and did not become statistics, so far as unemployment was concerned. They felt they were not employable.
All the young people decided to leave the area because jobs were not forthcoming and they, too, did not become statistics so far as unemployment is concerned. You would then imagine that the second wave of the criteria would apply, the one in respect of a family living in a non-urban population area and having an income of a predetermined figure. It is surprising, in an area where a large number of highly paid salesmen and a large number of teachers and professional people make their home and are not in the employee field, that a mockery is made of the family income, which is one of the criteria for the designation. It is more than surprising to those who know the area that the income in the Kirkland Lake area, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, is about $500 higher than the income in Noranda, and about $400 higher than the income in the Timmins area or vice-versa.
Progress reported.

PENITENTIARIES-REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF FEMALE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions in the past I have asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) whether he would consider the appointment of a female deputy commissioner within the penitentiaries system of Canada. At this time we need a modern approach to the problems of crime and punishment. This subject has been discussed on many occasions in the house over a number of years, and it is heartening to observe some signs that a change is taking place.
DEBATES	5911
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I am sure we are all looking for the initiation of a project which will protect society while at the same time, in so far as possible, encourage and help offenders to become useful members of our national community. I was greatly heartened to see the changes that have taken place in our prisons system when I was kindly invited to visit Cowansville in Quebec, where a new minimum security prison has been established. There have been many new changes made there in a physical way, different from the situation which existed in respect of the old bastille-like fortresses with which we have become familiar.
We have also been heartened by the minister's decision in the case of female drug offenders, in that they will not be sent back to Matsqui unless they so desire. On reflection, I am sure that many people will realize that this is a good move, in that the Matsqui prison is within a short distance of Vancouver, the worst drug centre in Canada, and that upon release of these prisoners they would more than likely be plunged back into this area.
It was also pleasing to note that recent newspaper reports indicate that a women's rehabilitation centre will be established in Kingston to be in full operation by August. The commissioner of penitentiaries stated that this centre would accommodate up to eight prisoners at one time and would be staffed by a superintendent, a female classification operator and four correction officers. He stated that prisoners at the prison for women in Kingston would be eligible for transfer to the home two months before the completion of their sentences.
All these things are signs that a change is in the making. Now is the time to make drastic changes in our method of treating women offenders, in line with the examples set by other countries of the world. I am sure that the appointment of a woman deputy commissioner within our penitentiaries system, to be in charge of all female offenders in female correctional institutions, including community hostels and prelease houses such as the one to be established at Kingston, will be a step in the right direction.
It is likely that the federal government will soon take over from the province the responsibility for all female offenders who have been sentenced to terms longer than one year. At the present time there are only about 120 women prisoners under federal care. It would seem suitable at this time to
5912	COMMONS DEBATES	June 2, 1966
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion try out a pilot plan under which some of the new ideas in penology, such as prelease houses, could be followed.
Women offenders, according to many penologists, are the best type of prisoner to use in trying out innovations. This is true because the majority are not involved in organized criminal society, are not dangerous to property or persons, and have been convicted for offences arising from inadequacy, prostitution, alcoholism, self-destruction and drug addiction. In other words, they are their own worst enemies and their own worst stumbling blocks to recovery.
This is not the place to discuss the details of the new penology nor the responsibilities of a woman deputy commissioner. These are set out very briefly and clearly in the submission recently prepared and placed before the government by the directors of the Elizabeth Fry Society of Kingston, Ontario, and the members of the senior staff of the prison for women at Kingston. I would simply urge upon the Solicitor General that there is need at this time for the appointment of a woman deputy commissioner within the penitentiaries system who would be charged with full responsibility for all female offenders in correctional institutions operated by the federal government.
I would very much hope that this step could be taken now, while the Solicitor General is freshly come to the problem. I really feel that Agnes MacPhail would be exceedingly happy and proud if she could see the fruition of so much of the work she tried to do more than 30 years ago, because she was trying to advance penology, as we are, among people of her time. It would seem to me that now, when we find that countries such as Holland, Japan, Britain and others have tried out something that is new and more modern in this respect, would be an excellent time to put in charge of female offenders a thoroughly capable woman commissioner, who might or might not live right on the spot-that is not important-but somebody who would be charged with the special responsibility to try out some of the newer methods of penology in this country, which is behind so many of the more advanced countries in this respect.

INCOME TAX-QUEBEC-IMPOSITION ON MONEY FOUND BY CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has to do with an item published in Le Nouveau Samedi of May 28, 1966, and entitled:
They find $30,000 while playing.
On May 30, 1966, I put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) concerning the contents of a woollen sock found on the street by two children in the city of Jonquiere.
The people of my area are asking a lot of questions on the source of this fabulous discovery of $30,000. At first glance one wonders whether this is not an amount hidden from the income tax by an individual or a corporation. But the serial numbers being consecutive, it can only involve a single withdrawal.
Indeed, the 300 $100 bank notes bear serial numbers A/J80,65600 to A/J80,65900 and are all brand new.
One could think that the amount was destined to a political party for the election campaign in Quebec. It could be an old trick used by some parties in spite of the promises made by the old politicians.
Yet, to top it all, a judge of the Superior Court of Quebec, Mr. Justice Toussaint McNicol, claims that he was holding the amount in trust but refuses to name the payee.
In that case it is the estate tax division which will have to intervene because this would be the first time in my life that I would be in a position to discover an estate in a woollen sock. Yet, there are those who claim that there are no more woollen socks in the province of Quebec.
It is said that out of the mouths of babes and sucklings comes the truth. Now, I would
June 2, 1966	COMMONS
be very pleased if those two candid babes could have contributed to throw some light on this very strange event.
And it had to happen right in the middle of the election campaign. Is it a consequence of the heat of the election?
What puzzles me most is the complete silence of most newspapermen about this event, they who are usually so fond of sensational news. Are we spectators at the comedy of the plague-stricken animals?
It is up to the Minister of National Revenue to see that the same justice is applied to all.
That is why I am asking the minister whether he intends to conduct a full inquiry into the matter.
